posts.text: Vickman @stratton001 Introducing STYX — built at NEAR HACKATHON on @NEARProtocol to bring scoped spending, delivery verification, and owner-controlled payments to agent services. As agents take on more useful work, one question becomes harder to ignore: how do we let them coordinate services without giving them unrestricted control over our money? An agent completing a task and a service requesting payment are only parts of the process. Someone still needs to define the rules, check what was delivered, and decide whether that delivery deserves payment. That is the workflow we built with STYX. HOW IT WORKS The current use case is turning structured invoices into accounting CSV files. An owner prepares a job and defines its scope, spending cap, permitted service, recipient, expiry, and delivery requirements. STYX compares service quotes and connects the selected work to those rules. The delivery then goes through deterministic checks for source coverage, arithmetic, duplicates, uncertainty, and integrity. The owner can inspect the actual CSV and verification results before accepting the work. For the NEAR testnet flow, the owner reviews and signs the relevant wallet actions. Buyer-agent, provider, and verifier roles use separate identities; they do not receive the owner’s wallet keys. A verified result can proceed to owner-approved payment. Failed checks block acceptance, and a reservation can be released without paying the provider. WHAT WE HAVE WORKING • Structured JSON/CSV invoice processing. • Local parsing, with optional NEAR AI extraction behind explicit data-sharing and API-cost consent. • Owner-defined rules and spending caps. • Service quote comparison. • Downloadable CSV deliveries and source comparisons. • Separate buyer-agent, provider, verifier, and owner roles. • NEAR testnet escrow, reservation, delivery, verification, and payment flows. • Transaction reconciliation that checks final receipts and contract state after interrupted or uncertain submissions. • Completed testnet payment and reservation-release examples. WHY BUILD THIS ON NEAR? STYX uses NEAR testnet to record and enforce the agreement and settlement flow, while keeping invoice contents off-chain. The application connects the work people can inspect with the payment actions owners authorize. A wallet redirect alone is not treated as settlement: STYX reconciles the transaction and contract state before reporting confirmation. The broader idea is a reusable pattern for agent services: bounded authority, inspectable delivery evidence, and explicit owner control over payment. TRY IT WITHOUT A WALLET We also built a public sample workspace so anyone can explore the product immediately. You can load 30 fictional invoices, set a spending cap, compare quotes, inspect the generated CSV, accept a successful delivery, or try an arithmetic-failure case and release the reservation. Each visitor gets an isolated temporary workspace. Sample payments are clearly labelled simulations and do not send NEAR. Separate proof links show earlier, actual NEAR testnet transactions. WHERE WE ARE TODAY STYX is a working testnet pilot. Both configured service providers are currently STYX-operated, and the verifier runs on a trusted server. The checks establish consistency with the supplied invoice data; they do not prove invoice authenticity. Independent security review, broader user testing, and operational hardening remain ahead before commercial use. We would love feedback from NEAR builders, agent developers, and people who work with invoice processing: what evidence would you need before allowing an agent-assisted workflow to release payment? Try STYX: usestyx.xyz Public sample: usestyx.xyz/try-demo Watch the walkthrough: youtu.be/7t0hImAfEIY Explore the code: github.com/vickman787/styx Delegate the work. Inspect the evidence. samimi @hassan_samimi AI agents can review invoices, extract financial information, and make payments. But giving an agent direct access to a wallet and its assets comes with serious risks. @Arashb122 and I worked on this exact problem with PrivatePay Agent. How can you allow an agent to make payments without giving it direct and unlimited control over assets??? In PrivatePay Agent, sensitive invoice information is first redacted locally. Only the sanitized text is then sent to NEAR AI Cloud Confidential TEE for processing. The Attestation report and the model response signature are also verified before the process continues. But the most important part happens at the payment stage. The agent has no token balance or direct access to the token contract. Instead, it can only call the try_pay method on a smart contract deployed on @NEARProtocol . Before making a payment, the contract checks predefined restrictions, including. ( 1- Daily payment limits 2- A list of approved recipient 3- Prevention of duplicate invoice payments 4- Verification of the agent identity and payment amount. ) If all checks pass, the contract executes the token transfer itself. If any restriction is violated, the payment is blocked and the failed attempt is recorded onchain. To use and test the project functionality, we built a CLI as the primary way to execute the workflow. We also developed a Web Dashboard where users can view successful payments, blocked attempts, and transaction statuses. ( The dashboard is read only and does not allow payments to be initiated ) The project has currently been implemented and tested on NEAR Testnet using the test token tUSDC. It is not yet ready for use with real assets or in a Mainnet environment. Our goal is to build a way for agents to perform specific financial tasks while keeping payment authority under verifiable restrictions. PrivatePay Agent Redacted locally. Attested in a TEE. As AI agents become capable of executing tasks, interacting with APIs, and working independently, one major challenge remains: How do we verify their work and ensure payments are settled fairly without relying on trust? That's what we're building with SETTLE. SETTLE combines on-chain escrow, programmable verification, and automated settlement into a system where payments are tied to predefined conditions rather than promises. Here's what we've built so far: • Smart Contract Escrow: Funds are locked on NEAR, with milestone-based releases governed by agreed conditions. • Programmable Verification: Supports API checks, GitHub CI, deterministic text validation, and human review for subjective deliverables. • Automated Settlement: Cryptographically signed verification results enable payouts after a challenge window. Today, the answer is blind trust. We built KAVREN to address this trust problem in the emerging agent economy for @NEARProtocol Hackathon 2026. KAVREN is a payment-assurance protocol for agent-to-agent work. Payment is tied to verified delivery: an agent gets paid only when its work meets the criteria agreed before the job began. How it works: → An owner funds a budget and sets the rules: spending limits, allowed providers, job types, expiry → A buyer agent works within those rules, gets a quote and hires a provider agent → Payment is locked in a NEAR smart-contract escrow → The provider agent plans the job with an LLM on NEAR AI Cloud; deterministic code carries out its decisions → An evaluator checks the delivered work against the agreed criteria → If it passes, payment becomes claimable by the provider. If it fails, the provider can retry. If time runs out, the escrow is refunded to the owner Any independent AI agent can use it. Through KAVREN's MCP server, Claude Desktop checked its budget, got a quote, hired a provider, monitored the job, then re-ran the evaluation itself before accepting the result. Built on: • Rust smart contracts on NEAR for escrow and payment enforcement • MCP for interoperability with independent AI agents • NEAR AI Cloud for the provider's LLM planning, with its TEE attestation verified by the evaluator • NEAR testnet and native NEAR for every transaction This is running infrastructure, not a concept. Every job agreements, verdicts and escrow/payment state are verifiable on-chain. Agents shouldn't need blind trust. Payment should follow proof. posts.author: xbtonchaine
posts.text:
Right now you mostly get two options.

Give the agent the keys, and one bad prompt or one bug can empty the wallet.

Or approve every payment yourself, and then it's not really an autonomous agent anymore.

Neither one scales.

posts.author: xbtonchaine
posts.text:
BILA sits in the middle.

You fund a treasury. You set the rules. The agent can only ask to spend from it.

A smart contract on NEAR checks every request and either approves it or blocks it.

The AI model never holds the money.

posts.author: xbtonchaine
posts.text:
What happens when a request comes in:

Inside the limits: approved, reserved, settled on chain.
Above the per-payment cap: blocked.
Small, but today's budget is already used: blocked.

The agent gets a plain reason back every time.

posts.author: xbtonchaine
posts.text:
Why the agent can't cheat:

Its key can only call one function, request_payment.
It can't attach money or change its own limits.
Raising a limit needs your wallet signature.
You can pause or revoke an agent any time, no deposit needed.

That's BILA. Live on Near.

posts.author: blasrodri
posts.text:
Making a market is expensive. Someone has to quote prices 24/7, commit capital, manage inventory and absorb risk.

For the long tail, the economics rarely make sense.

So I started with a question:

What if the market maker was just a formula?

posts.author: blasrodri
posts.text:
That's ZeroTick.

You bring a signed reference price with your trade.

The contract verifies it, computes an executable quote, and settles against a shared USDC vault.

No constantly posted on-chain quotes. No tokenized underlying. No dedicated liquidity pool per asset.

posts.author: blasrodri
posts.text:
Here's where it gets interesting.

The formula prices risk dynamically.

Stale data? Wider spreads.
Higher volatility? More expensive quotes.
Pool getting crowded? Prices adjust.
Risk limits hit? Trade rejected.
The pricing curve continuously adapts to protect liquidity.

posts.author: blasrodri
posts.text:
And every position has its maximum payout capped and reserved upfront.

The vault won't accept a trade it can't collateralize.

One pool can back many markets, with separate risk limits.

LPs don't need to seed every pair or actively post quotes.

That's the real innovation.

posts.author: blasrodri
posts.text:
Now consider the opportunity.

OTC Markets handled ~$691B in 2025.

Global FX trades ~$9.6 TRILLION a day.

Add niche equities, regional indices, commodities, and thousands of other assets with reliable prices but limited on-chain liquidity.

That's the universe we're going after

Bitcoin relies on cryptography that powerful quantum computers could eventually break.

Preparation matters.

What if people could prepare an escape route before quantum computers become a serious threat?
Without moving funds or giving up custody.
That's the idea behind Asylia.

posts.author: mielle_xol

We also built a watchman tracking 60 untouched Bitcoin wallets dating back to 2009.

Dormant wallets could become targets in a future quantum era, so we wanted to monitor what happens when one moves.

posts.author: mielle_xol
posts.text:
6/9
The watchman monitors these wallets for activity and triggers the configured release mechanism if one starts moving.

An early warning system for a threat affecting the wider ecosystem.

posts.author: mielle_xol
posts.text:
7/9
Why NEAR?
Asylia uses NEAR to seal and conditionally release signed escape transactions, exploring a preparation layer for Bitcoin and other ecosystems.

posts.author: mielle_xol

8/9
Quantum computers aren't cracking wallets today.
But vulnerabilities should be addressed before they become emergencies.
Asylia is our contribution to the conversation around quantum-resistant security.

posts.author: AlleManfredi
posts.text:
2/ The idea

NearCash is a physical banknote with a secure chip inside. The chip is the vault: it holds the key to the money.

You hand it to anyone like cash. Any phone with the NearCash app checks it's real and never spent, even offline.

posts.author: AlleManfredi
posts.text:
3/ How you get one

At a NearCash ATM you pick a banknote, choose a PIN and pay with almost any token, from almost any chain.

The ATM takes a blank note, its chip creates its own keys, the note is funded and certified by NEAR Chain Signatures, and it comes out ready to use.

posts.author: AlleManfredi
posts.text:
4/ Spending it

When you want, you redeem it back on-chain, to the token and chain you choose.

The chip signs one withdrawal and marks itself spent in the same step. After that it can never sign again: no
double spending.

The problem: a cap table is private, but a DAO still needs its vote to mean something exact

posts.author: 0Xuell

Confidential mode (zero-knowledge):

The chain stores only a sealed fingerprint of the cap table plus a Groth16 proof that it adds up. Who holds what never appears on chain.

The board checks its private copy before approving. Change one number and the check refuses it.

posts.author: 0Xuell

Payouts without exposing who owns what

A holder proves, in their own browser, that they're in the table and owed exactly their share, without saying which row is theirs. A relayer sends it to a brand-new account, so nothing links the payout to a named holder or to their wallet.

How a quake counts:
- USGS reports M6+ with an expected-impact alert of yellow or higher
- Five fixed bots check the official record on their own
- It counts only when 3 of the 5 attest the exact same record

A made-up quake stays pending and mints nothing.

posts.author: 0Xuell
posts.text:
What happens next: a small amount of new TREM is split between five fixed relief accounts.

Weekly and monthly caps limit how much can ever be created, so holders are diluted by a bounded amount.

posts.author: 0Xuell
posts.text:
Holders can also give their own coins to the relief list. A reserve of existing coins tops each gift up by 10%.

No new coins are created for that. The match goes to relief, not to the giver, and it has daily and monthly budgets.

posts.author: 0Xuell
posts.text:
Nobody can change the rules:
- no owner, admin or upgrade method
- publishers, parameters and relief list fixed at launch
- coin holdings never decide what counts

The page reads the contract live, including how many access keys remain.

We simulated it on 60 real days of USGS data before picking the numbers. Only 5 of the 28 M6+ quakes had enough expected impact to count.

Rust contract, Python reference and TypeScript engine agree on 28,537 steps across 200 scenarios.

What I built, a post-quantum route for QTC into NEAR Intents:

1. Lock QTC on Quantus in a 2-of-3 multisig, signed with ML-DSA-87
2. 2 of 3 attesters sign, and a contract with no admin key checks both signatures on-chain

posts.author: iamyacine

No classical key authorizes a mint or a release.

posts.author: Asqwe2411
posts.text: Evidence goes to a model on someone else’s server, and nobody can show where the analysis ran or that it wasn’t read. So I built the version I wanted to exist. Custos Seal analyzes evidence inside a NEAR AI Cloud confidential enclave and checks its attestation before it is sent.

posts.author: Asqwe2411
posts.text: Every finding becomes an on-chain receipt carrying the enclave’s signature, which the contract verifies. I wanted to use this stack properly: enclaves for the analysis, NEAR for the record, and a scoped key so even a stolen one can’t move funds.

posts.author: ogleksb
posts.text:
2/9 – The problem

Businesses process hundreds of invoices and payments.

Using AI can make this faster, but giving an AI agent direct access to company funds is risky.

One malicious invoice or prompt injection could lead to an unauthorized payment.

posts.author: ogleksb
posts.text:
3/9 – The idea

VaultGuard follows one simple principle:

Let AI do the thinking, but never give it control of the money.

AI analyses invoices and identifies risks. NEAR smart contracts independently enforce the rules before a payment can proceed.3/9 – The idea

posts.author: ogleksb
posts.text:
4/9  How it works
→ A business submits an invoice.
→ AI analyses it for suspicious information.
→ Vendor and recipient details are checked.
→ Spending limits and company policies are evaluated.
→ The NEAR smart contract independently checks whether the payment is authorized.

posts.author: ogleksb
posts.text:
5/9  What happens during an attack?
Imagine someone hides instructions in an invoice telling the AI to send $10,000 to an attacker's wallet.
Even if the AI recommends approval, the smart contract checks the actual payment details.
If the rules are broken, the payment is rejected.

posts.author: ogleksb
posts.text:
6/9 – What makes VaultGuard different?

→ AI-powered invoice analysis.

→ Restricted NEAR Function Call Keys.

→ Onchain spending limits and vendor controls.

→ Cryptographic attestations.

→ Cross-chain settlement through NEAR Intents 1Click.

→ Auditable payment activity.

posts.author: ogleksb
posts.text:
7/9 – Cross-chain payments

Once a payment passes the required checks, VaultGuard can use NEAR Intents 1Click to facilitate payments across supported blockchains.

Businesses can pay vendors in supported tokens without manually managing every blockchain transaction.

posts.author: ogleksb
posts.text:
8/9 – Security testing

We built a Security Center with 42 adversarial security checks covering:

Treasury custody attacks.
Attestation and TEE spoofing.
Cross-chain settlement attacks.

Our reported results: 42/42 passing security gates.

posts.author: ogleksb
posts.text:
9/9 – The bigger picture
The goal isn't to give AI more control over money.
It's to make AI-powered financial automation safer.
AI recommends. NEAR smart contracts authorize. The payment executor executes.
This is VaultGuard, built for the @NEARProtocol  Hackathon.
#NEARHackathon

Q1: How there's no relayer: a NEAR key can be limited to one method on one contract. We publish keys that can only call transact on the pool.

Anyone can submit a private transaction with them. Nobody can move funds with them.

posts.author: ringsonnear
posts.text:
Q2: Private swaps: the pool funds a brand-new single-use account. It swaps on Rhea, deposits the result back as a private note, and deletes itself.

NEAR to USDC, USDT, ZEC, RHEA and AURORA, live on mainnet.

posts.author: ringsonnear
posts.text:
Q3: AI agents: the agent runs on NEAR AI Cloud, and the app checks that its signing key lives in an Intel TDX enclave.

Spending caps are enforced in code, not by the model. In the demo it refused a tip hidden in a prompt injection.
